Guides

Portions, texture, and milk

Appetite is a better measure than a spoon count. Milk remains the main drink until the first birthday.

Findings

Start with teaspoons, then follow the baby. A few spoons one day and a whole bowl the next can both be normal.
Milk is still the largest part of the diet until 12 months. Food teaches iron and skill. It does not replace feeds on a schedule you invent.
Texture should be moving by eight or nine months. Water from an open cup can start with meals. Juice does not.

How much food

The first meals are practice as much as nutrition: one to three teaspoons, once a day, building toward two and then three meals. By the end of the first year many children are on three meals and two snacks, with portions that still vary wildly between children and between days.

Forcing the last spoons teaches a child to ignore fullness. So does offering food as a reward or as comfort for every upset. The division of responsibility is on the meals page: you decide what is offered, the child decides how much.

Where milk fits

Keep breast milk or formula on demand alongside meals. There is no need to drop a milk feed the day solids start. Toward the first birthday, food carries more of the iron and the milk feeds often settle into a morning, an evening, and perhaps one more.

After 12 months, drinks of milk at a volume much above 400 ml a day are a common reason a toddler will not eat. Offer water with meals. A bottle used as a constant sip can also pool milk on teeth.

Texture and cups

Smooth food at six months, mash and soft strips by eight or nine, and chopped family food by twelve is a fair arc. Individual babies move faster or slower. The risk is a child who reaches a year still on thin purée and then refuses lumps.

Offer sips of water in an open or free-flow cup with meals so drinking is practised. Juice, including diluted juice, is not a baby drink. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises no juice before 12 months.
